results.title: Minneapolis - Ratio of Households Living Above and Below the Poverty Line
results.description:
This map compares the number of households living above the poverty line to the number of households living below. In the U.S. overall, there are 6.2 households living above the poverty line for every 1 household living below. Green areas on the map have a higher than normal number of households living above compared to below poverty. Orange areas on the map have a higher than normal number of households living below the poverty line compared to those above in that same area.

In this map you see the ratio of households living above the poverty line to households living below the poverty line.  For the U.S. overall, there are 6.2 households living above the poverty line for every household living below. This map is shaded to clearly show which areas have about the same ratio as the U.S. overall, and which areas have far more families living above poverty or far more families living below poverty than "normal."

"The poverty rate is one of several socioeconomic indicators used by policy makers to evaluate economic conditions. It measures the percentage of people whose income fell below the poverty threshold. Federal and state governments use such estimates to allocate funds to local communities. Local communities use these estimates to identify the number of individuals or families eligible for various programs." Source: U.S. Census Bureau

The map shows the ratio for states, counties, tracts and block groups, using data from the U.S. Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) for 2013 for the previous 12 months.

results.title: The Ukrainian Cultural Landscape in Minnesota
results.description:
Ukrainians have been in Minnesota for quite a while. Did you know that over 16,000 Ukrainians are living in Minnesota right now? Although there are 16,000 Ukrainians in Minnesota not all of them have jobs, and jobs are very important to Ukrainians because that is what is supporting them and getting them money. There are only a few restaurants that are owned by Ukrainians. You should check out the map to see where they are. Also, there are only a few places that are doing Ukrainian events and holidays that get supported. You should look through the story map so you can learn about where these Ukrainians are and how they have changed Minnesota for the better! You will learn about the Jobs and Economy of Ukrainians, what Holidays and Traditions that Ukrainians have, Ukrainian Religion, and Ukrainian Food, Cuisine, and Agriculture. 

Process:

First We selected Ukrainian culture to explore in Minnesota. We were interested in learning about the history of migration and some of the cultural traits expressed in Minnesota. The first thing we did was create a map that had several layers related to the Ukrainian people and places in Minnesota. 

We used ArcGIS Online and Living Atlas to find pre-created layers:

  • European Ancestry → This layer helped us identify where in Minnesota people having Ukrainian background are located. We filtered the layer to show just Minnesota State and changed the style to show “Ukrainian” as the attribute to display by color counties. 

  •  Unemployment Rates → This layer helped us determine where the most unemployed people are in Minnesota. We filtered the layer to show only Minnesota state unemployment rates and changed the style to show where Ukrainians are most densely populated compared to the unemployment rates in Minnesota state.  

  • Where Urainians are in Minnesota → This layer helped us identify where Ukrainians are in Minnesota. We filtered the layer to show just Minnesota State and we changed the style to show “Ukrainian” as the feature to display by pinpointing counties. Then we filtered the layer to show Ukrainians in Minnesota. 

  • Food of Ukrainians in Minnesota (Our Handmade Layer) → This layer is a layer that we created ourselves to show specific places in Minnesota in which Ukrainians eat or farm. If you click on the points, it will show a detailed description of what the place is and more about it. The points range from markets, restaurants, and farms. 

  • Christian Churches and Churches of Christ Hot Spot → This layer is a Hot Spot of the layer U.S. Religion Census:Selected Data (2010) we filtered it to Minnesota and it shows where Christian Churches are most populated. 

  • Ukrainian Places in Minnesota (Our Handmade Layer) → This layer is a layer that we created ourselves to show specific places in Minnesota where Ukrainians are. If you click on the points, it will show a detailed description of what the place is and how it affects Ukrainians or how it is related to Ukrainians. The points range from gift shops, churches, stores, and community centers.

  • OpenStreetMap Churches in Minnesota → This layer is a layer that is in progress. We filtered this layer to show only Minnesota State. Then we filtered it to show Christian Churches and that is the cross symbol. 

We then created our own layer using a spreadsheet to display specific places in Minnesota where cultural elements of Ukrainian people can be observed. This layer is titled "Ukrainian Places in Minnesota (Our Handmade Layer)" and it shows places that Ukrainians work, go to practice their religion, and celebrate their holidays and traditions.  We chose to visualize this layer by cultural elements so the viewer can easily see which points on the map relate to where different Ukrainians work in Minnesota and where they celebrate different holidays and traditions.   

We created another of our own layers using a spreadsheet to display specific places in Minnesota where cultural elements of Ukrainian people can be observed. This layer is titled "Food of Ukrainians in Minnesota (Our Handmade Layer)" and it shows restaurants, markets, and farms in Minnesota that have Ukrainian food.   We chose to visualize this layer by cultural elements so the viewer can easily see which points on the map relate to the restaurants, farms, and markets we researched. 

Based on this map, We started to see a picture of Ukrainian culture in Minnesota.  We then did some more research about the background and migration history of how this group reached Minnesota.  We used MNOpedia as an initial resource and then utilized a variety of sources (attributed below) to research the three cultural elements We chose to research.  Ultimately, We used these cultural elements to evaluate the impact that Ukrainian people had on Minnesota’s cultural landscape. 

  • Jobs and Economy  - We wanted to learn more about where Ukrainians jobs are in Minnesota and how many jobs there are for Ukrainian people. We also wanted to know how many Ukrainians have jobs in Minnesota. 

  • Food, Cuisine, and Agriculture- We researched food, cuisine, and agriculture because we knew that food has a huge impact on most cultures. We wanted to evaluate what types of food Ukrainians eat and how that changes Minnesota's restaurants and farming styles.  

  • Religion- We researched Religion because we wanted to know more about Ukrainians religion that they practice and see if it is similar to the religion in Minnesota or if it is different. We were also interested in what kinds of Churches they went to.

  • Holidays and Traditions- We researched holidays and traditions because it ties in tightly with religion. When researching religion, we wanted to go in depth and research more. One of the ways we did this was learning about holidays and traditions and relating them to Ukrainian religion. 

Finally, We looked at all the layers and areas of cultural expression We found throughout Minnesota and tried to establish spatial relationships on the map, making conclusions from the patterns and connections we saw on the map.

results.title: Polish in Minnesota
results.description:
The Polish first came to Minnesota in the 1840s. They have continued to immigrate and bring their culture along with them until the late 1990s and the early 2000s. Most settled around the Twin Cities area and have impacted Minnesota greatly

In the 1600s, Poland was one of the largest countries in Europe. In that time period, there wasn't much ethnic and religious diversity, but in Poland, there was oddly a lot of diversity. In fact, up until World War I, Poland had one of the largest Jewish communities as well as German and Ukrainian.

Process

First I selected Polish culture to explore in Minnesota. I was interested in learning about the history of migration and some of the cultural traits expressed in Minnesota. The first thing I did was create a map that had several layers related to the Poles. 

I used ArcGIS Online and Living Atlas to find pre-created layers:

  • Polish Immigration → I chose this layer because it shows how MN has a greater Polish immigration rate than other states. 

  • ACS Language Spoken at Home Variables -Centroids → I chose this layer will relate to my ethnic group because you will be able to see the slow decline of Polish language in MN. I filtered this layer so that only Minnesota was shown.

  • ACS Children in Immigrant Families Variables→ I chose this layer because it can show how Polish immigrants are related to children nowadays. I filtered this layer so that only Minnesota was shown.

  • OpenStreetMap Places of Worship for North America→ I chose this layer because it gives a visual representation to the mention of a large number of Roman-catholic churches in the Twin Cities area. 

  • Farming, Fishing, and Forestry Employment and Wages - Metro or Nonmetro Areas → I chose this layer because most Polish Immigrants were farmers and some were a part of the forest industry. 

  • U.S. Legal Immigrants by Country of Birth from 1986 to 2012 →This layer benefits my map because it will show the decrease in Polish immigrants to the US due to the increase in the Polish economy. I filtered this layer so that it only shows Poland.

  • 2016 ACS Education Level by County→ This layer benefits my map because it shows the higher education level in the twin cities from an only 6 year old census which helps show the smarter polish immigrants that migrated more recently

I then created my own layer using a spreadsheet to display specific places in Minnesota where cultural elements of Polish people can be observed. This layer is titled "Polish Locations in Minnesota" and it shows specific places in Minnesota that relate to the Polish.  I chose to visualize this layer by cultural elements so the viewer easily see which points on the map relate to each cultural element I researched. 

Based on this map, I started to see a picture of Polish culture in Minnesota.  I then did some more research about the background and migration history of how this group reached Minnesota.  I used MNOpedia as an initial resource and then utilized a variety of sources (attributed below) to research the three cultural elements I chose to research.  Ultimately, I used these cultural elements to evaluate the impact that Polish people had on Minnesota’s cultural landscape. 

  • Agriculture and Food - I chose this element because when I was researching the Polish on the MNOpedia website, it mentioned farming a lot. I related this information back to agriculture and food. I started just by searching on google for the importance of agriculture and food to Polish in Minnesota. I then found what I thought was the best website and took my primary information off of there. 

  • Religion - I chose this element again because it was mentioned many times on the MNOpedia website. Most Polish immigrants were Roman-Catholic so I looked for different churches in Minnesota and took data from there. I also researched the importance of religion to Poles and I found that it related them back to Poland and let them rest for a while with different activities and calmness.

  • Dance and Music - I chose this element because two of the activities provided by churches were dancing and music. As I researched this element more, I found that dance and music were actually a very large part of Polish culture. I searched for an activity that had the two in Minnesota and found the Polish Fest in Minneapolis. 

Finally, I looked at all the layers and areas of cultural expression I found throughout Minnesota and tried to establish spatial relationships on the map, making conclusions from the patterns and connections I see on the map.
results.snippet: The Polish are a large part of Minnesota's history. Scroll to find out why!

results.title: A Cartographic Understanding of Poverty in Minnesota
results.description:
This story map will explore the geographic patterns of poverty across the state of Minnesota. The three maps will show poverty status at the state and county levels, which allows us to visually see and explore how poverty varies between different communities. The data used comes from the U.S. Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS), which was accessed through Esri's Living Atlas.

This is a map highlighting poverty levels in Hennepin County. I chose Hennepin County and Ramsey County for this story map because my house is in the Southeast area of Hennepin County, and it's just a couple of blocks from the Ramsey County border. As noted in the legend, the darker the shade of blue, the higher the percentage of people whose income in the past 12 months has been below the poverty level. Within Hennepin county, we can see that there is the most dark blue in the right east side of the county where the city of Minneapolis is located, while there is a lot more light blue in the surrounding areas where the suburbs are located.
results.snippet: Exploring Poverty in Minnesota at the State and County Levels

results.title: How Minnesotans get to Work
results.description:
This story map aims to show data on how people in the state of Minnesota, and more specifically in Mcleod and Carver counties, bordering counties Southeast of Minneapolis, get to work. Data for this project comes from the American community Survey (ACS), and was gathered from Esri's Living Atlas. The maps use percentage of workers that commute by driving alone, as it is the most common form of transportation to work.

Click on any county or census tract to see more information.

McLeod county map of transportation to work.

results.name: XCEL_Energy_Grid_Reliability_Minneapolis_Test_Map.mpkx
results.title: XCEL Energy Grid Reliability Minneapolis Test Map
results.description:
• This test map for the Minneapolis area was created for the purpose of providing an example of interactive map that contains certain Xcel Energy electric reliability and service quality data combined with demographic data from the US Census Bureau. The main goal is to demonstrate the interactive map design and to receive feedback from stakeholders before a final map is created for the complete Xcel Energy service territory.  The test map includes data only for the City of Minneapolis and any Census Block with 15 or less Xcel Energy Electric Premises has been excluded (the polygons have not been filled with color) to protect customer confidentiality and privacy.

    CELI 12 – Any Electric Premise that had an outage with a duration of 12 hours or more in one year.  The yearly average was derived by taking the total number of CELI 12 Premises from 2018 to 2020 per Census Block Group and dividing this total by three.  The percentage was obtained by dividing the yearly average by the total number of Electric Premises served by Xcel Energy in each Census Block Group.

    CEMI 6 – Any Electric Premise that had 6 or more sustained outages in one year.  The yearly average was derived by taking the total number of CEMI 6 Premises from 2018 to2020 per Census Block Group and dividing this total by three.  The percentage was obtained by dividing the yearly average by the total number of Electric Premises served by Xcel Energy in each Census Block Group.

    2019 Disconnections – This data includes any Electric Premise that was disconnected by Xcel Energy in 2019.  The percentage of disconnected customers per Census Block Group was derived by taking the count of 2019 disconnected premises in each Census Block Group and dividing this count by the total number of Electric Premises served by Xcel Energy in the same Census Block Group.

    The American Community Survey 5-Year Summary File was used for the US Census demographic data – Median Household Income, Percent People of Color (POC), and Poverty Rate. (American Community Survey 5-Year Summary File - Resources - Minnesota Geospatial Commons (mn.gov)

    • Median Household Income is the median income per household (MEDIANHHI).
    • Percent POC was derived by adding the Black Non-Hispanic (BLACKNH), American Indian Non-Hispanic (AMINDNH), Asian Non-Hispanic (ASIANNH), Pacific Islander Non-Hispanic (PACIFICNH), Other Non-Hispanic (OTHERNH), Multi-Racial Non-Hispanic (MULTRACENH), and Hispanic in combination with any race counts in this data set (HISPOP), and then dividing that count by the total population (POPTOTAL) for each Census Block Group.
    • Poverty Rate is the share of population with income at 0-184% of the federal poverty level per Census Block Group (POV185RATE).
